quests.hint: The vowel sounds like the one in 'bed'. Three letters in all.
quests.explanation: In three-letter words, the short /e/ sound is spelled with the letter e: pen, net, red. The vowel sits between two consonants.

quests.hint: Its vowel matches 'cup' and 'sun'; the final sound is /s/.
quests.explanation: Short /ʌ/ in a small word is spelled u: bus, cup, sun. The closing /s/ is written with a plain s, not z or c.

quests.hint: Short /o/ as in 'hot' and 'top'. The middle letter isn't an a.
quests.explanation: Short /o/ is spelled o in words like job, hot and top. Some accents say it closer to /ɑ/, which can tempt you toward 'a', but the spelling stays o.

quests.hint: It rhymes with 'kiss' and finishes with the same double letter.
quests.explanation: One-syllable words with a short vowel usually double a final s, f or l: boss, dress, stuff, hill. Teachers call this the FLOSS pattern.

quests.hint: It rhymes with 'tell'. Check how that word ends.
quests.explanation: The same doubling applies to l after a short vowel: doll, spell, shall. A few short words break the pattern, such as 'pal'.

quests.hint: The opposite of 'on'. Watch out for the look-alike word 'of'.
quests.explanation: 'Off' follows the doubling pattern (cliff, sniff, off). 'Of' is a different word, and one of the very few where the letter f sounds like /v/.

quests.hint: It opens with one sound written as two letters, then a short vowel.
quests.explanation: The digraph sh stands for a single sound, /ʃ/. Compare 'stop', where s and t are two separate sounds; in sh, the two letters fuse into one.

quests.hint: The same /ʃ/ sound, now at the end, right after a short i.
quests.explanation: The sh digraph can close a word as easily as open one: wish, dish, cash, fresh. After the short vowel, nothing extra is needed.

quests.hint: It means 'a lot' and ends with the /tʃ/ of 'chip', written with just two letters.
quests.explanation: Spelling /tʃ/ as tch is common after short vowels (match, patch), but a few words end in plain ch: much, such, rich.

quests.hint: It starts with a tongue-between-teeth sound and ends like 'bank'.
quests.explanation: Before k, the /ŋ/ sound is written with n, not ng: think, bank, drink. The th at the start is a digraph for one sound.

quests.hint: This question word opens with the same two letters as 'what' and 'why'.
quests.explanation: The h in wh- is easy to lose because most speakers just say /w/. It still has to be written: when, where, which.

quests.hint: Only four letters, and it ends in the same digraph as 'bath'. It is a very small linking word.
quests.explanation: The digraph th ends this small word: two letters, one sound, always in the order t then h.

quests.hint: The letter q never travels alone. After a short i, the final /k/ takes two letters.
quests.explanation: In ordinary English words q is followed by u, and qu says /kw/: quick, quiet, queen. The word then closes with ck after its short vowel.

quests.hint: It rhymes with 'snack': a short a, then a final /k/ sound.
quests.explanation: After a short vowel at the end of a word, /k/ is normally ck: pick, sock, duck. A plain k follows a consonant or a long vowel instead (milk, bank, week).

quests.hint: Two different spellings of /k/ appear in this word: one at the start, one at the end.
quests.explanation: Use c for the opening /k/ before l, and ck for the closing /k/. The ck digraph never begins a word, so 'klok' and 'cloc' both go wrong.

quests.hint: One box, two ___. The plural needs an extra syllable you can hear.
quests.explanation: Nouns ending in x, s, z, sh or ch (as in 'church') form the plural with -es: box → boxes. The added e is the extra syllable.

quests.hint: One plan, three ___. Nothing about the base word changes.
quests.explanation: Most plurals just take -s: plan → plans, trip → trips. Save -es for endings you can't follow with an s without adding a syllable.

quests.hint: The singular already ends in a double s, and the plural is a whole syllable longer.
quests.explanation: The singular 'class' keeps both s letters, and the plural adds -es on top: class → classes. Nothing is dropped.

quests.hint: After the short a, the /tʃ/ sound needs three letters.
quests.explanation: After a short vowel, /tʃ/ is usually written tch: match, patch, watch. Very few common words break this: much, such, rich, which.

quests.hint: Three consonants and then a final e follow the short i.
quests.explanation: After a short vowel, word-final /dʒ/ is spelled -dge: bridge, edge, badge. The final e is silent, and it signals that the g is soft.

quests.hint: It has the same /tʃ/ spelling as 'catch', but here it sits in the middle of the word.
quests.explanation: The tch pattern also works inside words after a short vowel: kitchen, pitcher, itchy. Don't confuse it with 'chicken', where the /k/ comes from ck.

quests.hint: Add the ending to the whole base word: nothing dropped, nothing doubled.
quests.explanation: When a base word ends in two consonants (lp), -ing goes straight on: helping, jumping, sending. Doubling and e-dropping don't apply here.

quests.hint: The end sounds like /t/, but the past-tense spelling still uses two letters.
quests.explanation: Regular past tense is written -ed even when it sounds like /t/ (asked, jumped) or /d/ (played). It never ends in a plain t.

quests.hint: The past-tense ending adds a full syllable here, and the vowel after w doesn't sound like an a.
quests.explanation: The -ed ending is pronounced /ɪd/ after t or d (wanted, needed, started). After w, the letter a often sounds like /ɒ/, as in wash and watch, yet it is still written a.

quests.hint: Long a in the middle of the word, spelled with two vowels.
quests.explanation: Inside a syllable, /eɪ/ is commonly spelled ai: train, rain, wait. Words seldom end in ai, so a different spelling appears at the end.

quests.hint: Long a at the very end of the word. Choose the spelling that finishes words.
quests.explanation: At the end of a word, /eɪ/ is spelled ay: day, say, way. English words rarely end in ai.

quests.hint: It means 'perhaps'. The first syllable rhymes with 'day' and uses the same ending spelling.
quests.explanation: The ay closes the first syllable (may-be), so it keeps the ay spelling even in the middle of the written word. Syllable position matters, not just word position.

quests.hint: It starts with th, and the nasal before the k is written the way it is in 'think'.
quests.explanation: The n-before-k pattern returns: /ŋk/ is written nk. The final s belongs to this form: you thank someone, but you give thanks.

quests.hint: It begins with a word for beach grains, and the second half is spelled like 'which'.
quests.explanation: The final /tʃ/ is plain ch, not tch: another short-vowel exception, like much and which. Many speakers skip the d in casual speech, but it stays in the spelling: sand + wich.

quests.hint: A short coat. The /k/ that closes the first syllable is spelled the same way as in 'back' and 'clock'.
quests.explanation: The ck digraph also works in the middle of a word when a short vowel is followed by the next syllable: jacket, pocket, packet. A plain k would be wrong here.
